report:55627.t: The committee looked at the threats facing UK water, such as rivers and lakes, including pollution from farming and sewage. It also looked at wider worries, such as whether water supplies can cope with problems and whether there will be enough water in future.

report:55631.t: The committee looked at the cost and running of the work to restore and renew the Palace of Westminster. More than a million people visit it each year, and it is a world heritage site known for its Victorian neo-gothic design.

report:55567.t: The committee looked at how hair and beauty products and treatments are made safe and regulated. Products can harm people if they contain ingredients that are not regulated, and treatments can harm people if they are not carried out properly.

report:55591.t: The committee looked at planning rules for nuclear fusion, the process that powers the Sun. The Government has decided the technology has advanced enough to bring in planning law that would help prototypes and demonstration sites get built.

report:55592.t: The committee looked at how the Government deals with China on trade and the economy. It weighed the possible gains for the UK from closer economic ties against the risks that closer ties could bring.

report:55581.t: The committee looked at food and weight management in England, including treatments for obesity. In 2022, 64% of adults in England were overweight or living with obesity.

report:55582.t: The committee looked at the money position of the British Council, which promotes UK culture, education and the English language around the world. It is a public body backed by the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office and was founded 90 years ago.

report:55523.t: The committee looked at Sizewell C, a planned large nuclear power station on the Suffolk coast. The government is paying for it with the energy company EDF and private finance, and it is expected to cost between £40.5bn and £47.7bn.

report:55506.t: The committee looked at two reports the Parliamentary and Health Service Ombudsman laid in September 2025. Each came from an investigation into a complaint about the Charity Commission for England and Wales.

report:55495.t: The committee looked at food and weight management in England, including treatments for obesity. In 2022, 64% of adults in England were overweight or living with obesity.

report:55447.t: The committee looked at the threats in the High North, the Arctic region, now and in future. It asked what the UK's defence and security interests are there, and whether the UK has the right plans, equipment and allies to deal with them, especially threats from Russia.

report:55397.t: The committee looked at wildfires and how to manage the risk. The UK is facing more frequent and more severe storms, floods, heatwaves and wildfires, which put public health, infrastructure, food production and nature at growing risk.

report:55412.t: The committee looked at how UK Research and Innovation spends money on research buildings and equipment. The Government wants the UK to be one of the top three places in the world to start and grow a technology business by 2035, and this body is central to that aim.

report:55313.t: The committee looked at fixed links, such as bridges or tunnels, to Scotland's islands. Transport matters to island communities because it supports local businesses and access to essential services, while poor links can limit travel and contribute to people leaving.

report:55254.t: The committee published a report on the agreement about Gibraltar between the European Union and the UK. It was published on 14 October 2026 and debated in Grand Committee on 20 October 2026.

report:55121.t: The committee looked at the future of the BBC as part of the review of its Royal Charter. The Charter sets out how the BBC is run, regulated and paid for, and it is reviewed about every ten years.

report:55105.t: The committee looked at how well the Office for Budget Responsibility works and what its record has been. It also asked whether the body should change, and if so how.

report:55076.t: The committee looked at the threats facing UK water, including pollution from farming and sewage. It also looked at wider worries, such as whether water supplies can cope with problems and whether there will be enough water in future.

report:55075.t: The committee looked at the Government's step in to keep British Steel going. The UK steel industry has been under pressure from rising energy prices, the move to cleaner production, trade uncertainty and global competition. In January 2026 the company employed 4,052 permanent staff.

report:55056.t: The committee looked at how the UK can change the way it makes and uses energy. It asked how the Government can bring people along, as vocal opposition to net zero has grown and political agreement on it has broken down.

report:55059.t: The committee looked at UK International Climate Finance, money the UK gives to help other countries deal with climate change. It started in 2011 and helps the UK meet its duties under the Paris Climate Agreement.

report:55061.t: The committee looked at UK International Climate Finance, money the UK gives to help other countries deal with climate change. It started in 2011 and helps the UK meet its duties under the Paris Climate Agreement. This is the large print version of the report.

report:54977.t: The committee looked at how Scotland's economy and workers can gain from more UK defence spending. The Government has committed to raise defence spending to 2.6% of national income by 2027, and the inquiry focused on creating highly skilled jobs.

report:54971.t: The committee looked at what rules might be needed to protect human rights as AI is developed and used, and what that might mean for future laws. Many people argue AI can bring benefits, such as helping with decisions and making work more productive.

report:54942.t: The committee held a hearing before the Chair of the Care Quality Commission was appointed. This is known as a pre-appointment hearing.

report:54964.t: The committee looked at how water, energy and broadband are regulated. Its earlier work found that the water regulators had left a failing sector to struggle, and that digital inequality was adding to economic inequality.

report:54958.t: The committee looked at how well the UK Statistics Authority is doing its job. That includes its two executive offices, the Office for National Statistics and the Office for Statistics Regulation.

report:54978.t: The committee looked at the health effects of breast implants and other cosmetic procedures. It asked how safe and how well regulated surgical and non-surgical procedures are, including how the risks are explained and managed.

report:54979.t: The committee looked at the health effects of breast implants and other cosmetic procedures. It asked how safe and how well regulated surgical and non-surgical procedures are, including how the risks are explained and managed. This is the large print version of the report.

report:54849.t: The committee looked at government compensation schemes. When public bodies fail and harm people, those people should expect fair and quick compensation, but the committee's earlier reports on the Windrush, Equitable Life and British Steel Pension schemes found failings.

report:54743.t: The committee looked at plans to grow Northern Ireland's economy, including the UK Industrial Strategy. It paid particular attention to new sectors that could become the industries of the future.

report:54780.t: The committee checked the Northern Ireland Troubles Bill against human rights standards. The Bill was introduced in the House of Commons on 14 October 2025 and would repeal and replace parts of an earlier 2023 Act on dealing with the legacy of the Troubles.

report:54620.t: The committee looked at how well the human rights of children in England are protected when they are in the social care system.

report:54621.t: The committee looked at how well the human rights of children in England are protected when they are in the social care system. This is the Easy Read version of the report.

report:54592.t: The committee looked at pet parasite medication, such as flea and tick treatments, especially those containing the pesticides fipronil and imidacloprid. It asked how these products reach the environment and what using or not using them means for wildlife and human health.

report:54558.t: The committee looked at a major data breach by the Ministry of Defence in February 2022. It involved the personal data of thousands of Afghans who had applied to be resettled in the UK, and their families, and could have put them at risk of reprisals.

report:54402.t: The committee looked at young people who are not in work, education or training. Nearly one million people aged 16 to 24 are in this position, which can harm their prospects and wellbeing.

report:54321.t: The committee looked at why fewer children are reading for pleasure. Reading brings many benefits to children, young people and their families, and the committee asked what can be done to reverse the decline.

report:54322.t: The committee held a hearing before the new Chief Inspector of Constabulary and Fire and Rescue Authorities was appointed. This person makes sure police forces and fire and rescue authorities are inspected and reports publicly on how efficient and effective they are.

report:54342.t: The committee looked at how advice and legal services are adapting so people can get access to justice in civil, criminal and family law. It also looked at the effects of the cyber-attack on the Legal Aid Agency.

report:54344.t: The committee looked at how the Government is trying to free up land for building homes. The Government says a shortage of land underlies the housing crisis, and the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government runs programmes to increase the supply.

report:54203.t: The committee looked at food and weight management in England, including treatments for obesity. In 2022, 64% of adults in England were overweight or living with obesity.

report:54217.t: The committee looked at how government departments share back-office services such as human resources and payroll. Since 2004, the Government has tried to bring these functions together to cut costs and make data more consistent.

report:54237.t: The committee looked at why Black people face a higher risk of homelessness. It also looked at what the Government should include in its coming strategy on homelessness and rough sleeping, which covers several departments.

report:54240.t: The committee looked at why Black people face a higher risk of homelessness. It also looked at what the Government should include in its coming strategy on homelessness and rough sleeping. This is the large print version of the report.

report:54178.t: The committee looked at the UK's development partnership with Nigeria. In 2023 Nigeria was the sixth largest recipient of UK aid, with over £100m, down from third place in 2022 when it received £110m.

report:54171.t: The committee looked at the Government's new Financial Inclusion Strategy. It sets out plans to make it easier for people across the UK to get financial products and services.

report:54168.t: The committee looked at why historic buildings and places matter in the UK and what stops them being preserved. It asked about funding, and whether the current ways of paying for this are suitable and easy to use.

report:54139.t: The committee looked at people approaching State Pension age. When the age last went up, more people aged 60 or over but below pension age fell into poverty, and this group is among the poorest of working-age adults.

report:54140.t: The committee looked at whether large businesses pay the right tax. They bring in around 40% of the tax HM Revenue and Customs collects, though they are less than 0.1% of UK businesses. HMRC works with about 2,000 of them, typically those with turnover above £200m.

report:54020.t: The committee looked at how science and research can help the UK abroad. It asked how they support the Government's growth missions, increase the UK's international influence and help national security.

report:54019.t: The committee looked at student loans. Tuition fees for higher education were first brought in by the Government in 1998. Since then the cost to students has risen, and so has the amount they can borrow through student loans.

report:54000.t: The committee carried out its twice-yearly check on the UK-US trade and economic agreements. Since its last report, the Economic Prosperity Deal has been extended through a Technology Prosperity Deal and an agreement on pharmaceutical tariffs.

report:53980.t: The committee looked at the Independent Commission on Adult Social Care, led by Baroness Louise Casey, which was launched on 29 April 2025. The Commission is expected to make clear recommendations for an adult social care system that meets current and future needs.

report:53987.t: The committee looked at the condition of homes in England, in the private rented sector.

report:53897.t: The committee looked at Northern Powerhouse Rail. Since 2014, successive governments have accepted that rail in the North of England is limited, and several large cities, including Leeds, Liverpool, Manchester, Newcastle and Sheffield, are poorly served by transport links.

report:53768.t: The committee looked at how financially secure government-sponsored museums and galleries are. Fifteen national museums and galleries, including the British Museum and the Science Museum, are sponsored by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport, and free access to their permanent collections is provided as a result.

report:53604.t: The committee looked at why disabled people are less likely to be in work, a gap that has stayed at nearly 30%. The Government plans to spend an extra £2.2 billion on employment support over the next four years, and the committee scrutinised those programmes.

report:53726.t: The committee looked at UK-EU relations. At a Joint Summit in May 2025 the UK and EU agreed a Security and Defence Partnership. Progress since then has been limited, with core areas for agreement still to be concluded.

report:53718.t: The committee looked at a draft order to change the Human Rights Act 1998 on judicial immunity. The Act says that when a judge acts in good faith, damages can be awarded only in two circumstances. The first is to compensate someone for being deprived of their liberty.

report:53602.t: The committee looked at community energy and how it could help speed up the move to cleaner energy.

report:53577.t: The committee looked at the Health Bill, which was introduced in the House of Commons on 14 May 2026. Its main purpose would be to abolish NHS England and move its functions to other bodies or to the Department of Health and Social Care, including some powers going directly to the Secretary of State.

report:53578.t: The committee looked at the Access to Work scheme. The Department for Work and Pensions pays for and runs it, and it has helped disabled people and those with health conditions since it began in 1994.

report:53510.t: The committee looked at the Courts and Tribunals Bill, which was introduced in the House of Commons on 25 February 2026. Its Second Reading debate was due on 10 March, and dates for the next stage were yet to be confirmed.

report:53523.t: The committee looked at how regulation affects growth. Done well, regulation can be essential for promoting growth and investment. Done badly, it can hold investment back and stop growth.

report:53519.t: The committee looked at how taxis and private hire vehicles are licensed. They are a key part of the transport network, but the rules can vary between licensing authorities, which creates inconsistencies and raises questions about how effective the standards are.

report:53466.t: The committee looked at how affordable it is to buy a home. It focused on people buying a home for themselves and their families to live in, rather than on people buying to rent out or as an investment.

report:53467.t: The committee looked at prisons, probation and rehabilitation in Wales. These are the responsibility of the UK Government, while health, education and housing are devolved to the Welsh Government. Wales has five adult male prisons and a young offender institution, but no prison for adult women.

report:53440.t: The committee looked at how to boost investment in the UK economy. The Government has made economic growth its number one mission, but the UK has lagged behind its peers, and in 2025 the IMF projected UK growth of just 1.2%.

report:53461.t: The committee followed up on the Ministry of Defence's accounts. In November 2025 the National Audit Office gave a qualified opinion on the 2024-25 accounts, which found £1.5bn of legacy projects at the Atomic Weapons Establishment whose value had stayed the same for several years.

report:53413.t: The committee looked at the future of the veterinary workforce. Animal and plant diseases and pests have wide effects on the environment, farming, trade, human health, animal welfare and the food we eat.

report:53438.t: The committee looked at the asylum system. In December 2024 the Government committed to restore order to it, with changes that included the UK-France treaty on illegal crossings and a pilot one in, one out scheme for returning failed asylum seekers.

report:53321.t: The committee looked at stablecoins, a type of digital currency, and how they might be regulated in the UK. It asked whether they could disrupt traditional banking and payments services.

report:53342.t: The committee looked at support for people with frailty outside hospitals. More than one in ten people over 65 and up to half of those over 85 live with frailty, which is strongly linked to ageing and raises the risk of falls and of needing hospital or long-term care.

report:53352.t: The committee looked at how the Government is moving to digital services. After the general election, the Department for Science, Innovation and Technology announced plans to become the digital centre of government.

report:53275.t: The committee looked at how the Ministry of Defence tackles economic crime and misconduct. It investigates fraud and corruption against it through several police forces and its own central team. Its last public estimate of its exposure to fraud risk was £1.3bn in 2021-22.

report:53249.t: The committee looked at the draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, which the Government published on 27 January 2026. The Government asked it to check whether the proposed reforms would work and what changes could improve the draft before the final version goes to Parliament.

report:53273.t: The committee looked at the draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, which the Government published on 27 January 2026. The Government asked it to check whether the reforms would work and what could improve the draft. This is the large print version of the report.

report:53529.t: The committee looked at the draft Commonhold and Leasehold Reform Bill, which the Government published on 27 January 2026. The Government asked it to check whether the reforms would work and what could improve the draft. This is the Easy Read version of the report.

report:53253.t: The committee looked at policing and security in Northern Ireland. 2026 marks 25 years since the PSNI was set up following the Patten review, and the inquiry asked how far the review's aims have been met and what challenges remain today.

report:53252.t: The committee looked at how to attract inward investment to Wales. This means investment from one country in another that gives the investor a lasting interest in a business, usually by owning 10% or more of its shares.

report:53257.t: The committee looked at how to attract inward investment to Wales. This means investment from one country in another that gives the investor a lasting interest in a business, usually by owning 10% or more of its shares. This is the Welsh-language summary of the report.

report:53229.t: The committee looked at competition and how well the market works in the UK live music industry. That included the part played by the CMA, the competition regulator, in overseeing the sector.

report:53187.t: The committee looked at how physical activity can improve the health and wellbeing of older people. Progress on healthy life expectancy in England has stalled, and people are spending longer living with ill health in their older years.

report:53188.t: The committee looked at how physical activity can improve the health and wellbeing of older people. Progress on healthy life expectancy in England has stalled, and people are spending longer living with ill health in later life. This is the large print version of the report.

report:53197.t: The committee looked at the National Audit Office's financial audits. It audits over 400 public organisations that oversee £1.2 trillion of spending, and checks that their accounts are true and fair and that money is spent and collected as Parliament intended.

report:53144.t: The committee looked at how drought is managed in England, and whether current policies are enough for present and future droughts. It covered the effects of drought, monitoring, engagement and changes in water supply and demand, to find ways to be better prepared.

report:53147.t: The committee looked at why disabled people are less likely to be in work, a gap that has stayed at nearly 30%. The Government plans to spend an extra £2.2 billion on employment support over the next four years, and the committee scrutinised those programmes.

report:53167.t: The committee looked at why disabled people are less likely to be in work, a gap that has stayed at nearly 30%. The Government plans to spend an extra £2.2 billion on employment support over the next four years. This is the audio summary of the report.

report:53182.t: The committee looked at why disabled people are less likely to be in work, a gap that has stayed at nearly 30%. The Government plans to spend an extra £2.2 billion on employment support over the next four years. This is the British Sign Language summary of the report.

report:53099.t: The committee looked at the Government's plans for digital ID. Digital ID can cover many parts of a person's identity stored digitally, such as names, digital versions of documents like visas, or even a fingerprint or face scan.

report:53044.t: The committee looked at the health and wellbeing services available to people who work in Parliament. It asked how existing services can be better explained and supported, and where some needs are still not being met.

report:52983.t: The committee looked at the money problems facing universities and the role of international students. Dozens of universities are making redundancies and cutting courses to stay afloat, amid uncertainty over where their money will come from.

report:52987.t: The committee published its report on how regulators can support growth on 12 May 2026. The Government replied on 14 July 2026, and the report was debated on 3 November 2026.

report:52959.t: The committee looked at the failures at South East Water, and at wider threats to UK water, including pollution from farming and sewage. It also looked at worries about whether water supplies can cope with problems and whether there will be enough water in future.

report:52865.t: The committee looked at the Bank of England's plan to renew the system that moves large payments between banks. The system, known as RTGS, underpins UK payment systems including BACS and Visa and processes around £750bn a day.

report:52831.t: The committee looked at AUKUS, a security agreement between Australia, the US and the UK announced in 2021. Under it, the US and UK will help Australia get a fleet of nuclear-powered submarines, and the three countries will work more closely on other advanced military technology.

report:52837.t: The committee looked at the UK's fiscal framework, which is meant to keep public finances sustainable. It includes a set of fiscal rules and the arrangements for checking how the Government is performing against those rules.

report:52824.t: The committee looked at how the UK can keep delivering high-impact international aid in the face of a 40% budget cut, as the Government seeks to pay for higher defence spending in the name of national security.

report:52821.t: The committee looked at how the Government deals with fishing communities. After leaving the EU, the UK negotiates as an independent coastal state to agree fishing limits and quotas for fish stocks it shares with other countries, while balancing pressures on the marine environment.

report:52818.t: The committee looked at how accountable small government bodies are. To make sure public money is spent and managed well, departments and arms-length bodies must meet many standards, including annual reporting and rules on governance, planning and delivery.

report:52776.t: The committee looked at the risks from PFAS, a large group of about 14,000 man-made chemicals used in everyday products. They keep food from sticking to packaging or cookware, make clothes and carpets resist stains, and make firefighting foam more effective.

report:52715.t: The committee looked at the condition of homes in England, focusing on temporary accommodation.

report:52742.t: The committee looked at the future of relations between the UK and the US.

report:52760.t: The committee looked at the New Hospital Programme, announced in 2020 with a commitment to build 40 new hospitals by 2030. In January 2025 the Government confirmed that all schemes would go ahead, including replacing seven hospitals built with a weak type of concrete known as RAAC.

report:52665.t: The committee looked at the health of sport in local communities and schools and whether more can be done to grow sporting opportunities for everyone. It looked at funding, how volunteers can be better supported and how to open up grassroots sport to under-represented groups.

report:52645.t: The committee ran a fan-led review of live and electronic music, launched in June 2025 and independently chaired by Lord Brennan of Canton. It brought music lovers together to discuss ideas to protect the industry and make sure it works in the best interests of fans.

report:52458.t: The committee looked at what drives extremism in the UK, especially young people being drawn into extremism, violence and crime through online radicalisation. It asked whether the Government's approach is keeping pace and how effective measures such as Prevent are.

report:52441.t: The committee looked at the future of HMP Parc. In Wales, prisons, probation and rehabilitation are the responsibility of the UK Government, while health, education and housing are devolved. Wales has five adult male prisons and a young offender institution but no prison for adult women.

report:52395.t: The committee looked at historical forced adoption. In July 2022 the Joint Committee on Human Rights published a report on the adoption of children of unmarried women between 1949 and 1976, which examined adoption practices in England and Wales at that time.

report:52401.t: The committee looked at how hostile states and other groups use disinformation to undermine democracy. It tried to find out who is mainly responsible and which channels and technologies they use, to map their motives and locations, and to understand the impact of artificial intelligence.

report:52388.t: The committee looked at the National Security Strategy, which the Government published on 24 June 2025. It reviews the risks facing the UK and sets out plans to deal with them under three themes: security at home, strength abroad, and sovereign and asymmetric capabilities.

report:52403.t: The committee looked at how the Government uses data analytics to catch error and fraud. The Government lost between £55bn and £81bn to fraud and error in 2023-24. Central platforms used to detect them generated around £400m of savings in the same year.

report:52327.t: The committee looked at environmental regulation. Regulation is one of the main tools the Government is using for its Environmental Improvement Plan, and it says it intends to streamline regulation to protect nature and drive economic growth.

report:52277.t: The committee set up a panel of experts, politically impartial and independent of the committee, to evaluate palliative care in England. The panel produces a report after each evaluation, which is sent to the committee to review.

report:52272.t: The committee looked at how the UK Government is including the needs and voices of women in its development work. It explored the Women, Peace and Security agenda adopted by the United Nations and how it is built into UK aid, as the aid budget is planned to be cut to 0.3% of national income by 2027.

report:52276.t: The committee looked at how the UK Government is including the needs and voices of women in its development work. It explored the Women, Peace and Security agenda adopted by the United Nations. This is the large print version of the report.

report:52264.t: The committee looked at plans to grow Northern Ireland's economy, including the UK Industrial Strategy. It paid particular attention to new and emerging sectors, which are described as the industries of the future.

report:52249.t: The committee looked at the effects of coastal erosion on communities. The UK is facing more frequent and severe storms, floods, heatwaves and wildfires, which put public health, infrastructure, food production and nature at growing risk.

report:52190.t: The committee looked at the finances of adult hospices in England. In 2023 total UK hospice income was £1.8bn, with around £0.5bn from the state and the rest from charity. In 2023-24 many hospices said they might have to cut services by up to 20% without extra funding.

report:52138.t: The committee looked at the Government's planned changes to who can get Indefinite Leave to Remain, also known as settlement. It asked for the evidence on the changes and their likely impact, to feed into the new policy as it is developed.

report:52132.t: The committee looked at the BBC World Service, which had a weekly audience of 320m in 2023-24. Since 2022 the BBC has cut spending on it, partly because of falling licence fee income, with savings plans of £28.5m announced across its international services.

report:52134.t: The committee looked at the role of the UK's innovation system in helping to grow the economy across the whole country. This is part of the Government's mission to kickstart economic growth.

report:52061.t: The committee looked at how the Government uses external consultants. It intends to halve spending on them and has committed to producing a strategic workforce plan for the civil service in 2025 to balance the use of civil servants and outside help.

report:52040.t: The committee looked at AI, copyright and the creative industries. It explored the practical steps that would let creators reserve and enforce their rights against AI systems, how open AI developers should be, and how licensing, credit and labelling tools could support a fair market for creative work.

report:52039.t: The committee looked at transport for children to school. Many children and young people with special educational needs and disabilities must travel long distances to schools that can meet their needs.

report:51956.t: The committee looked at the advice on the Seventh Carbon Budget from the Climate Change Committee. It considered the assumptions and costs behind the advice, the balance between new and established technologies, the choices facing the Government, and the likely effects on households, businesses and the economy.

report:51939.t: The committee looked at the Government's proposed reset of the UK's relationship with the European Union.

report:51954.t: The committee looked at the Whole of Government Accounts, which bring together the accounts of over 10,000 public organisations, including departments, councils, the NHS and devolved administrations, to give the most complete picture of the UK's public finances. In 2022-23 the National Audit Office was unable to sign them for the first time ever.

report:51887.t: The committee followed up its earlier work on women's reproductive health, focusing on the needs of girls and young women. It assessed progress on diagnosis, treatment and pain management for conditions including endometriosis, adenomyosis and heavy menstrual bleeding.

report:51817.t: The committee questioned Doug Gurr, a former head of Amazon UK, on Tuesday 24 February to judge whether he was suitable to be Chair of the Competition and Markets Authority. It then prepared a report on the appointment, before the Secretary of State confirmed him in the post.

report:51721.t: The committee heard from West Midlands Police and the West Midlands Police and Crime Commissioner about the decision to stop Maccabi Tel Aviv fans attending the match against Aston Villa in November 2025. It explored the intelligence behind the decision, the options police considered, and the political context.

report:51713.t: The committee looked at the health effects of breast implants and other cosmetic procedures. It asked how safe and how well regulated surgical and non-surgical procedures are, including how the risks are explained and managed.

report:51714.t: The committee looked at the health effects of breast implants and other cosmetic procedures. It asked how safe and how well regulated surgical and non-surgical procedures are, including how the risks are explained and managed. This is the large print version of the report.

report:51712.t: The House of Lords committee carried out a short inquiry into forensic science, following up on its 2019 inquiry and on recent work from the Westminster Commission on Forensic Science, which described the sector as being in a graveyard spiral.

report:51662.t: The committee looked at the transformation of National Savings and Investments, which borrows for the Government from savers through products such as premium bonds. It has around 25m savers with over £230bn invested, and is replacing Atos as its single supplier with several suppliers.

report:51536.t: The committee looked at the Government's plans for a Small Business Strategy. At the Autumn Budget 2024 the Government said it would publish a strategy setting out its vision for supporting small businesses, due in 2025.

report:51534.t: The committee held a one-off session on replacing RAAC in schools. It followed up on the RAAC crisis in the summer of 2023 and the work by the Department for Education and schools to deal with faulty, worn-out concrete, and looked more widely at how school buildings are managed.

report:51539.t: The committee looked at fraud and error in benefit spending. In 2023-24 the Department for Work and Pensions spent £268.5bn on benefits and pensions, and the National Audit Office reported overpayments of £9.7bn, the highest ever in cash terms, mostly in Universal Credit.

report:51518.t: The committee looked at how investment in the railway is planned, known as investment pipelines.

report:51519.t: The committee looked at the Railways Bill, which the Government introduced to bring running the rail network and looking after its infrastructure under a single organisation, Great British Railways. A separate Public Bill Committee goes through the Bill line by line.

report:51493.t: The committee looked at the condition of homes in England, focusing on the social rented sector.

report:51492.t: The committee held a session on the final report of Operation Kenova, published on 9 December 2025. It followed up on the earlier committee's look at the interim report, published on 8 March 2024.

report:51434.t: The committee looked at the UK-EU agreement on food and farming standards, known as an SPS agreement. Animal and plant diseases and pests have wide effects on the environment, farming, trade, human health, animal welfare and the food we eat.

report:51458.t: The committee looked at how the UK can keep delivering high-impact international aid in the face of a 40% budget cut, as the Government seeks to pay for higher defence spending in the name of national security. This was an interim report.

report:51386.t: The committee looked at how efficient and resilient the Probation Service is. Reforms in 2014 split it in two, and were heavily criticised, so it was brought back together in 2021 to build a more sustainable system.

report:51370.t: The committee looked at why medicine shortages are growing across England, which affect patients' health and put pressure on the NHS, pharmacies and GPs. It also looked at how well the UK can predict and prevent supply problems and limit harm to patients.

report:51366.t: The committee looked at the UK-India trade agreement after it was announced. It investigated the terms of the deal, its possible benefits and disadvantages for the UK, and how its key provisions will work for important sectors.

report:51334.t: The committee looked at the cost of clinical negligence claims. In 2025 it found it unacceptable that the Department of Health and Social Care had no plan to deal with these costs, with so much taxpayers' money going on legal fees.

report:51305.t: The committee held a one-off session on gendered Islamophobia. It aimed to understand the particular challenges facing Muslim women in the UK today.

report:51310.t: The committee held a one-off session on gendered Islamophobia. It aimed to understand the particular challenges facing Muslim women in the UK today. This is the large print version of the report.

report:51276.t: The committee looked at how to make policing more productive. Police funding in 2025-26 is £19.6bn, about 70% from central government and the rest from council tax. The Government aims to put 13,000 more officers and staff into neighbourhood policing.

report:51283.t: The committee looked at the skills needed for transport manufacturing, such as cars, buses, aeroplanes, trains and ships. Manufacturers are worried about skills shortages, so the committee asked what skills are needed now and later, and how the Government can help.

report:51210.t: The committee looked at faulty energy efficiency work in people's homes. Two government schemes, ECO4 and the Great British Insulation Scheme, are paid for through energy bills and fit improvements such as insulation.

report:51183.t: The committee looked at the first 1000 days of life, from conception to age two, which are widely seen as a critical period for child development. The previous committee looked at this in 2019, considering national strategy, spending and barriers to investment and local services.

report:51167.t: The committee looked at the UK's trade deals with its three most important partners: the United States, India and the European Union. It looked closely at the detail and rollout of the India trade deal, the US-UK Economic Prosperity Deal and what was agreed at the UK-EU Summit.

report:51128.t: The committee looked at how UK financial services can take advantage of AI while limiting threats to financial stability. It also looked at how to protect financial customers, particularly vulnerable ones.

report:51065.t: The committee looked at the finances of children's care homes. The number of looked after children rose by 19% to 83,360 between 2015-16 and 2023-24, and around 16% of them live in children's homes.

report:51008.t: The committee looked at the growth of private markets in the UK after reforms brought in following 2008. It asked whether those reforms have made banks less able or willing to lend, pushing risk away from banks and towards private markets.

report:50888.t: The committee followed up on its recent scrutiny of the Department for Work and Pensions in autumn 2025. Its report in July 2025 on Jobcentres warned that the Government seemed complacent about the effect of reduced support for people claiming benefits.

report:50887.t: The committee followed up on its recent scrutiny of the Ministry of Justice in autumn 2025. Its 2024 report on legal aid expressed deep concern about a lack of curiosity over how fewer providers affects people's access to legal aid, though evidence suggests access is getting harder.

report:50844.t: The committee looked at how the UK can prepare for an ageing society. The birth rate is falling and life expectancy is rising, so the UK can expect older people to make up a growing share of the population.

report:50681.t: The committee looked at how government manages fees and charges to recover the cost of providing services, and how it identifies those costs to improve productivity. Better productivity is key to the Government's aim of making public services more affordable.

report:50722.t: The committee published its report on the Building Safety Regulator on 11 December 2025. The Government replied on 11 February 2026.

report:50674.t: The committee looked at how accessible the House of Commons is. Accessibility was one of the topics most often raised in its call for views, and the inquiry covered both the buildings and Parliament's procedures, language and information.

report:50625.t: The committee looked at how government manages fees and charges to recover the cost of providing services, and how it identifies those costs to improve productivity. Better productivity is key to the Government's aim of making public services more affordable.

report:50584.t: The committee looked at how to build the workforce needed to deliver the policies and infrastructure for the UK's clean, secure energy mission.

report:50484.t: The committee looked at community mental health services. It examined what good looks like from the point of view of the people who use the services and their families and carers.

report:50478.t: The committee looked at Government policy on dealing with the legacy of the past in Northern Ireland. On 4 December 2024 the Secretary of State announced the next steps to repeal and replace the Northern Ireland Troubles (Legacy and Reconciliation) Act 2023.

report:50289.t: The committee looked at the BBC's accounts. On average 85% of UK adults use the BBC each week, spending 6hr26min watching BBC TV or iPlayer. In 2023-24 there were 23.9 million TV licences in force, around 775,000 of them free licences for people over 75.

report:50297.t: The committee published its report on the rule of law on 20 November 2025. The Government replied on 23 February 2026.

report:50252.t: The committee looked at the UK's contribution to European security. That included its part in NATO and its defence relationships with individual European countries.

report:50242.t: The committee looked at how to cut NHS waiting times for planned, non-emergency care. The standard is that 92% of patients should start treatment within 18 weeks, but at the end of 2024 patients on 59% of pathways, or 4.4m people, were waiting less than 18 weeks.

report:50248.t: The committee held a session on rates of sexually transmitted infections, including among particular groups, and on how well the Government's strategies are working to reduce them. It also covered HIV and access to PrEP, a medicine that helps prevent HIV.

report:50226.t: The committee looked at access to energy for communities in developing countries. Energy is at the core of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the 2015 Paris Agreement on Climate Change, yet the world is largely off track in meeting these commitments.

report:50227.t: The committee looked at access to energy for communities in developing countries. Energy is at the core of the 2030 Agenda for Sustainable Development and the 2015 Paris Agreement on Climate Change, yet the world is largely off track. This is the large print version of the report.

report:50209.t: The committee looked at resettlement and rehabilitation, investigating the cycle of reoffending. HM Prison and Probation Service aims to reduce reoffending by rehabilitating the people in its care through education and employment.

report:50195.t: The committee looked at the Afghanistan Response Route, set up by the Ministry of Defence to reduce the security risks after a data breach in February 2022 in which personal information about Afghan citizens was disclosed without permission. The National Audit Office published a report to support the committee's scrutiny.

report:50196.t: The committee looked at the Government's proposal for a revised National Policy Statement for Ports.

report:50125.t: The committee looked at the reset of UK-EU relations that the Government is pursuing. It had two main themes: what the reset is or should be, and how the Government goes about it with the EU, including the role of interested parties in the UK.

report:50123.t: The committee looked at the cost of maintaining the Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office's overseas estate. It covers over 6,000 properties in almost 180 countries, valued at around £2.5 billion, and each presents its own challenges, from supply issues to security concerns.

report:50127.t: The committee looked at the challenges and opportunities for farming in Wales. In 2022 agriculture, fishing and forestry made up 1.8% of employment in Wales, and over 90% of the land area of Wales is used for farming.

report:50043.t: The committee looked at how well the UK can withstand threats from animal disease. The National Risk Register lists the most serious risks facing the UK, and in 2023 it included four animal diseases.

si:rGFxGHHw.t: This law uses powers in the Seafarers (Wages and Working Conditions) Act 2023, which lets ministers make rules on pay and working conditions for seafarers working on certain services.

si:mIlXGLPt.t: Lighthouse authorities are allowed to borrow money, with the total outstanding limited to £100 million. This Order is about increasing that borrowing limit.

si:fp2KAkLc.t: This law changes the rules on employment tribunals. People who want to bring a claim must first contact ACAS, and this law adds to the information they have to give ACAS when they do. It also clarifies the 2014 rules and adds detail on early conciliation.

si:17TytsXp.t: This law extends by 12 months a temporary arrangement that lets certain Gibraltar-based firms provide financial services in the UK. It also helps similar UK firms to reach Gibraltar's financial services market.

si:Kwm1hCVo.t: This law changes the Export Control Order 2008 and an EU rule of 5 May 2009 that controls the export, transfer, brokering and transit of dual-use items, meaning goods that can have both civilian and military uses.

si:cAuHizF6.t: An earlier set of regulations gave eight jobs to the Chartered Trading Standards Institute: approving and overseeing the providers that settle consumer disputes without going to court. This law amends the rules on information and fees connected to that role.

si:tWGs34ly.t: This law requires certain people and organisations to give specified data to HM Revenue and Customs on an ongoing basis.

si:YoM1py2V.t: This law updates a customs rule to point to a new version of a document that lowers import duty on nine types of steel goods. They are used to make bright bar, a precision-finished steel bar, and wire.

si:gTlMeqyh.t: This law changes the Control of Asbestos Regulations 2012. After asbestos work is finished, the check that the premises are clean must now be done by someone appointed independently of the person who did the work.

si:95geQdk5.t: This law changes the levy that supports the Contracts for Difference scheme. Government money can already be paid in to reduce the levy, and this law widens the circumstances in which that can happen.

si:jwkIB2GR.t: This Order puts into law a scheme from the Charity Commission for England and Wales for running the Russell-Cotes Art Gallery and Museum charity. Before it, the charity was governed by a section of the Bournemouth Borough Council Act 1985 and its governing documents.

si:UjLJSYiY.t: This law says which types of people count as an approved person under the Transport Act 2000 for the purposes of assessing bus franchising.

si:bXdaajgS.t: This law creates a new independent body, the Adult Social Care Negotiating Body for England, under the Employment Rights Act 2025. It also sets out how the body will operate.

si:AFeUMktt.t: This law lets certain public authorities charge fees for services they provide on some transport infrastructure projects. It uses powers added to the Highways Act 1980 and the Transport and Works Act 1992 by the Planning and Infrastructure Act 2025.

si:3esVEoaz.t: This law changes three sets of rules on how applications, objections and inquiries are handled under the Transport and Works system. Some transitional arrangements apply.

si:mkqed3xX.t: This law changes the rules on sea fishing that came from the EU and were carried over into UK law. It also includes a temporary arrangement for the changeover.

si:ii3dQqwx.t: This Order changes the electoral arrangements for North Somerset, following recommendations from the Local Government Boundary Commission for England. It does not change the boundary of the district itself.

si:OiSurC7C.t: This Order changes the electoral arrangements for Herefordshire, following recommendations from the Local Government Boundary Commission for England. It does not change the boundary of the district itself.

si:YPJC25UA.t: This law follows on from the English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026, which sets up the Local Audit Office. It makes staff of the new office eligible to join the Local Government Pension Scheme.

si:Y1gTgO0j.t: This law adds the College of Policing to the list of organisations covered by the law enforcement part of the Data Protection Act 2018. The College's handling of personal data now falls under those rules.

si:ZkVUN2LW.t: This law sets out the Treasury's decisions that the rules covering certain clearing houses, known as central counterparties, in Indonesia and the People's Republic of China are equivalent to UK rules.

si:wEh0GMpE.t: This law changes the Individual Savings Account Regulations 1998 as they apply to Lifetime ISAs.

si:lK2XwjUW.t: This Order puts certain drugs under the control of the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971, following advice from the Advisory Council on the Misuse of Drugs. Drugs are classed as A, B or C, and the class affects the criminal penalties for offences involving them.

si:4gHVF4Al.t: This law changes the Family Procedure Rules 2010, the rules on how family court cases are run.

si:087Tamhz.t: This Order brings into effect on 30 October 2026 a revised Code of Practice on access and unfair practices when trade unions seek recognition or derecognition at a workplace. It replaces the earlier Code of Practice that came into effect on 1 October 2005.

si:OTdpcDRu.t: The Pension Schemes Act 2026 creates a new public pension scheme for members of the AWE Pension Scheme and moves the scheme's assets to government. This law lets the Secretary of State direct that the assets be transferred to central government.

si:jzuhpM3V.t: This Order follows on from the Trusts and Succession (Scotland) Act 2024, which excludes pension schemes set up under a trust. That is because regulating occupational and personal pension schemes is reserved to the UK Parliament under the Scotland Act 1998.

si:UGFy2gNY.t: This law changes the rules for Northern Ireland Assembly and local elections so that both can be held together on 6 May 2027, if the Chief Electoral Officer decides they should be.

si:xfBCA4Pu.t: This law replaces technical standards for eCall, the system that automatically calls emergency services after a crash, to include 4G and 5G versions. Existing standards stay in use until 2G networks close.

si:pfGmswEG.t: This Order raises the maximum penalty for breaking a customs rule from £2,500 to £10,000. No Tax Information and Impact Note was prepared because it makes no substantive change to tax policy.

si:xsIP1eap.t: The English Devolution and Community Empowerment Act 2026 changes how mayoral combined authorities and mayoral combined county authorities issue precepts. This law makes the changes that follow from that.

si:Qo71QUEt.t: This law sets out the prison sanctions that Crown Court judges can impose on an offender for contempt of court after they breach an order to attend a sentencing hearing. They reflect the punishments a prison governor can impose for breaking prison discipline.

si:Mt1SX3Ny.t: This law changes the rules on appeals to the First-tier Tribunal against certain notices issued under the marine licensing system.

si:Ez8N3KGd.t: This law changes two sets of marine licensing rules: the list of activities that are exempt from needing a licence, and the fees charged for applications.

si:BZoUQWsP.t: This law names South West Grid for Learning Trust as a suitable body to report intimate images to internet service providers and internet access providers.

si:UWRQji9C.t: This law removes certain social security benefits from people detained in hospital under the Mental Health Act 1983, or the equivalent Scottish law, after they have been convicted of a serious offence.

si:zNOasVYT.t: This Order gives legal effect to the agreement between the UK Government and the North Atlantic Salmon Conservation Organization on its headquarters, as later amended.

si:u6KEN9sY.t: This law changes the rules on activities, including storing waste, that can be carried out in England without an environmental permit if the operator meets certain requirements and conditions.

si:t8PzHUjl.t: This law makes changes to other laws that follow from the new rules on subscription contracts coming into force under the Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024.

si:HZwMqBMU.t: This Order sets 30 October 2026 as the day a Code of Practice on the right of trade unions to access workplaces comes into effect.

si:O48wrvwG.t: This law sets out how the Director General of the Independent Office for Police Conduct oversees complaints and other matters about the conduct of authorised investigators who work for the Cabinet Office in the Public Sector Fraud Authority.

si:fo9x6Gm8.t: This law changes the rules of the Upper Tribunal. An Online Safety Act appeal must be brought within 3 months of OFCOM publishing the decision. It also changes how immigration judicial review cases are handled, and gives parties 12 working days to apply to appeal.

si:FND47L09.t: This Order lists the Clerk and Deputy Clerks of the Sexual Offences Court as offices in the Scottish Administration that are not ministerial offices for the purposes of the Scotland Act 1998.

si:8GQmOk2P.t: This Order removes a reference to the Scottish Ministers' functions under section 44 of the Climate Change (Scotland) Act 2009, because no functions under that section could be exercised by way of arrangements under the Scotland Act 1998.

si:eKdtUO6m.t: This Order sets the pay of school teachers in England, along with other conditions of employment that relate to their professional duties and working time.

si:fFr2MkcO.t: This law changes the Welfare Food Regulations 1996, which set up the Nursery Milk Scheme. The scheme gives children under five one-third of a pint of milk (189ml) on any day they are in childcare with an approved provider for two hours or more.

si:xBWbMKJR.t: This Order, made at the request of the Port of Tyne Authority, modernises and brings together the legal powers that apply to the port. It includes an updated constitution for the Authority.

si:PV3Gy6jF.t: This law changes the Pay As You Earn rules so that loans and living accommodation count as a specified benefit. It also sets out how to work out their cash value for PAYE.

si:1i95iUkI.t: The First-tier Tribunal and Upper Tribunal (Chambers) Order 2010 organises these tribunals into chambers and decides which chamber handles which work. This Order amends it.

si:u6J7p6rv.t: This law sets out what charges local authorities can make for certain building-related work.

si:xKlmWTGl.t: This law is made under powers in an EU regulation of 20 June 2019 on persistent organic pollutants, a group of harmful chemicals.

si:oxd3CEry.t: Local housing authorities can make empty dwelling management orders for homes that are wholly unoccupied. An interim order lets the authority take steps to make sure the home becomes, and stays, occupied. This Order amends the rules for these orders.

si:goOxDhpt.t: This law lets the Secretary of State require certain authorities to give them information about anti-social behaviour, which may include reports they receive and how they responded.

si:F4L6NQJl.t: Northern Ireland Assembly elections are held on the first Thursday in May every five years. The old Assembly must be dissolved at the start of a minimum period before the election, and this Order, made by the Secretary of State, amends how that period is set.
